[[Kardecist Spiritualism|Kardecist]] and Western [[New Age]] reinterpretations of karma frequently cast it as a sort of luck which is associated with virtue: if one does good or spiritually valuable acts, one deserves and can expect good luck; conversely, if one does harmful things, one can expect bad luck or unfortunate happenings. In this conception, karma is affiliated with the [[Neopaganism|Neopagan]] ''law of return'' or ''Threefold Law,'' the idea that the beneficial or harmful effects one has on the world will return to oneself. There's also the metaphysical idea that, because karma is a force of nature and not a sentient creature capable of making value judgments, karma isn't about good and evil deeds, since applying those labels would require those judgments, but about positive and negative energy, where negative energy can include things not seen as "being bad" like sadness and fear, and positive energy can be caused by being creative and solving problems as well as by exuding love and doing virtuous acts. This conception of karma handles the big problem with the more traditional view, because it explains why bad things happen to people who've done nothing "wrong"; it's all due to the sort of energy they've sent out into the universe with their thoughts and feelings, which exert as much power as actual actions. This view of karma, which centers around the idea that all things are made of karmic energy and thus able to affect each other, is referred to as "omniverse karma" or "omni-karma" because it requires the existence of an [[omniverse]] (a space which contains all the universes) as portrayed by [[superstring theory]], with which it closely agrees, and includes concepts such as souls, psychic energy, [[synchronicity]] (a concept originally from [[Carl Jung]], which says that things that happen at the same time are related), and ideas from quantum and theoretical physics (such as that time doesn't exist as we think it does). ==See also== *[[Edgar Cayce on Karma]] *[[Just-world phenomenon]] *[[Karma in Hinduism]] *[[Sin]] *[[Theosophy]] *[[Yuanfen]] *[[Esoteric Christianity]] ===References and Related Links=== † Cited from ''Dancing with Siva'' by [[Satguru Sivaya Subramuniyaswami]] *[http://www.veda.harekrsna.cz/encyclopedia/dharma.htm Dharma-Karma-Samsara] *[http://www.lioncity.net/buddhism/lofiversion/index.php/t10692.html Karma In Buddhism] *[http://swami-center.org/en/chpt/ecology/page_7.shtml Destiny and Its Correction] *[http://www.exoticindiaart.com/article/karma Exploring Karma - Tales of a Universal Principle] *[http://www.photonics.cusat.edu/article2.html Karma and the laws of Quantam Mechanics] *[http://www.lawofkarma.net/lpjarun/index.html Law of Karma - Dhamma Practice Book Series, by Luang Poh Jarun of Wat Amphawan, Thailand]

:''This article is about the religious concept. For other uses, see [[Karma (disambiguation)]]'' :''Basic definition'': '''Karma''' is a concept of [[eastern religions]] about the entire cycle of [[cause and effect]]. Simply explained, it is a sum of all that an individual has once done during many lives and is currently doing. The effects of those deeds actively create present and future experiences, thus making one responsible for one's own life. '''Karma''' ([[Sanskrit]]: कर्म from the root kri, "to do", meaning ''deed'') or '''Kamma''' ([[Pali]]: meaning ''action, effect, destiny''). In Hinduism and, later, Buddhism, it is the sum of a person's actions, regarded as determining that person's future states of existence. The law of '''Karma''' originated in the [[Vedic religion|Vedic]] system of religion, otherwise known as [[Hinduism]] or ''Sanatan Dharma'' (perennial faith). As a term, it can at the latest be traced back to the early [[Upanishads]], around [[1500s BC|1500 BC]]. == Karma in the [[Dharma]]-based religions == ===Hinduism=== :''See main article, [[Karma in Hinduism]]'' The concept of Karma, based on the [[Vedas]] and [[Upanishads]] was a concept that was adopted by other religions like [[Buddhism]] and [[Jainism]]. One of the first and most dramatic illustrations of Karma can be found in the great Hindu [[epic]], the [[Mahabharata]]. The original Hindu concept of karma was later enhanced by several other movements within the religion, most notably [[Vedanta]], and [[Tantra]]. Karma literally means "deed" or "act" and more broadly names the universal principle of [[cause]] and [[effect]], action and reaction which governs all life. Karma is not fate, for man acts with free will creating his own destiny. According to the Vedas, if we sow [[Goodness and value theory|goodness]], we will reap goodness; if we sow [[evil]], we will reap evil. Karma refers to the totality of our actions and their concommitant reactions in this and previous lives, all of which determines our future. The conquest of karma lies in intelligent action and dispassionate reaction. Not all karmas rebound immediately. Some accumulate and return unexpectedly in this or other births. As †Satguru Sivaya Subramuniyaswami explains it, unkindness yields spoiled fruits, called [[papa]] and good deeds bring forth sweet fruits, called [[punya]]. He further notes that as one acts, so does he become. One becomes virtuous by virtuous action, bad by bad action. It is considered an entirely impersonal and spiritually originated law that cannot be abrogated by any person. The thought of karma as punishment or being retributive is incorrect, as it is simply an extended expression of natural acts. The effects experienced are also able to be mitigated by actions and are not necessarily fateful. Societal groups as nations and their populations incur collective karma, and personalities incur individual karma. ====Three Kinds of Karma==== * There are three types of karma, *# [[sanchita karma]], the sum total of past karmas yet to be resolved; *# [[prarabdha karma]], that portion of sanchita karma that is to be experienced in this life; and *# [[kriyamana karma]], the karma that humans are currently creating and will bear fruit in the future. Notably, Karma in Hinduism, which differs from Buddhism and Jainism, involves the role of [[God]]. For a detailed look at such a role, please see [[Karma in Hinduism]]. ===Buddhism=== In Buddhism, only intentional actions are karmic "acts of [[Will (philosophy)|will]]". The 'Law of Karma' refers to "cause and effect", but Karma literally means "action" - often indicating intent or cause. Accompanying this usually is a separate tenet called [[Vipaka]], meaning result or effect. The re-action or effect can itself also influence an action, and in this way, the chain of causation continues [[ad infinitum]]. When Buddhists talk about karma, they are normally referring to karma/action that is 'tainted' with ignorance - karma that continues to ensure that the being remains in the everlasting cycle of [[samsara]]. This samsaric karma comes in two 'flavours' - 'good' karma, which leads to positive/pleasurable experiences, like high rebirth (as a [[deva]], [[asura]], or [[human]]), and bad karma which leads to suffering and low rebirth (as a [[hell]]-sufferer, as a [[preta]], or as an animal). There is also a completely different type of karma that is neither good nor bad, but liberating. This karma allows for the individual to break the uncontrolled cycle of rebirth which always implies suffering, and thereby leave [[samsara]] to permanently enter [[Nirvana]]. The Buddhist [[sutra]]s explain that in order to generate liberating karma, we must first develop incredibly powerful concentration, and proper insight into the (un)reality of samsara. This concentration is akin to the states of mind required to be reborn in the Deva realm, and in itself depends upon a very deep training in ethical self-discipline. This differentiation between good karma and liberating karma has been used by some scholars to argue that the development of [[Tantra]] depended upon Buddhist ideas and philosophies. Karma is related to the notion of [[Rebirth (Buddhist)|Buddhist rebirth]] - sometimes understood to be the same thing as [[reincarnation]] - which has its roots in the principle of Karma. ===Jainism=== Jains believe that karma is a form of [[matter]]. [[Mahavira]] described karma as "[[clay]] [[particle]]s". Jains do not believe in "good karma" or "bad karma"; they try to avoid all karma. ===Parallels with Christianity=== [[Christian]] teachings do not usually include the idea of Karma, although some parallels can be made, such as in the [[ethic of reciprocity|Golden Rule]] and as exemplified by biblical verses: :God is not mocked, what a man sows he must reap ''and'' "[[Vengeance]] is mine" says the Lord. Christianity is saturated with the concept of poetic justice not only from scripture but also in colloquialisms such as: "What goes around comes around." "Good things happen to good people." "You reap what you sow." Karma is thought by some [[Society of Jesus|Jesuit]] theologians to be consistent with the doctrine of [[Purgatory|purgatory]]. For other Christians however, the idea of the [[Abrahamic God]] makes the concept of Karma redundant. Most interpretations of [[Christianity]] do not emphasize the religious importance of thoughts and intentions ([[volition]]), that are usually understood to be a major form of Karma by the doctrines that use that concept. From the Bible we read: "For as he thinketh in his heart, so is he." (Proverbs 23:7) From the Book of Mormon we read: "But this much I can tell you, that if ye do not watch yourselves, and your thoughts, and your words, and your deeds . . . ye must perish. And now, O man, remember, and perish not." (Mosiah 4:30) ===Surat Shabda Yoga=== The [[Surat Shabd Yoga|Surat Shabda Yoga]] traditions describe four types of karma. To those listed under ''[[#Three Kinds of Karma|Three Kinds of Karma]]'' (above), it adds: Adi karma (original karma)—karma not earned but given by the Divine as the soul descends into the lower creation. == Western Interpretation == An academic and religious definition was mentioned above. Although Karma cannot be proven as easily as the law of [[gravity]], millions of people believe in it and is a part of many cultures and the psyches of millions of people. Others without religious backgrounds, especially in western cultures or with Christian upbringings, become convinced of the existence of Karma. For some, karma is a more reasonable concept than eternal damnation for the wicked. [[Spirituality]] or a belief that virtue is rewarded and sin creates suffering eventually leads to a belief in Karma. According to Karma, performance of positive action results with the reaction of a good conditioning in one's experience, whereas a negative action results in a reaction of a bad response. This may be an immediate result following the act, or a delayed result occurring either in the present life or the next. Thus, meritorious acts may create rebirth into a higher station, such as a superior human being or a godlike being, while evil acts result in rebirth as a human living in less desirable circumstances, or as a lower animal. Some observers have compared the action of karma to [[Western civilization|Western]] notions of [[sin]] and judgment by [[God]] or gods, while others understand karma as an inherent principle of the Universe without the intervention of any supernatural Being. In [[Hinduism]], God does play a role and is seen as a dispenser of karma; see [[Karma in Hinduism]] for more details. The latter understanding is accurate with regard to [[Buddhism]] and [[Jainism]]. Most teachings say that for common mortals, having an involvement with Karma is an unavoidable part of day-to-day living. However, in light of the Hindu philosophical school of [[Vedanta]], as well as [[Gautama Buddha]]'s teachings, one is advised to either avoid, control or become mindful of the effects of desires and aversions as a way to moderate or change one's karma (or, more accurately, one's karmic results). ===New Age and Theosophy=== The idea of karma was popularized in the west through the work of the [[Theosophical Society]]. [[Kardecist Spiritualism|Kardecist]] and Western [[New Age]] reinterpretations of karma frequently cast it as a sort of luck which is associated with virtue: if one does good or spiritually valuable acts, one deserves and can expect good luck; conversely, if one does harmful things, one can expect bad luck or unfortunate happenings. In this conception, karma is affiliated with the [[Neopaganism|Neopagan]] ''law of return'' or ''Threefold Law,'' the idea that the beneficial or harmful effects one has on the world will return to oneself. There's also the metaphysical idea that, because karma is a force of nature and not a sentient creature capable of making value judgments, karma isn't about good and evil deeds, since applying those labels would require those judgments, but about positive and negative energy, where negative energy can include things not seen as "being bad" like sadness and fear, and positive energy can be caused by being creative and solving problems as well as by exuding love and doing virtuous acts. This conception of karma handles the big problem with the more traditional view, because it explains why bad things happen to people who've done nothing "wrong"; it's all due to the sort of energy they've sent out into the universe with their thoughts and feelings, which exert as much power as actual actions. This view of karma, which centers around the idea that all things are made of karmic energy and thus able to affect each other, is referred to as "omniverse karma" or "omni-karma" because it requires the existence of an [[omniverse]] (a space which contains all the universes) as portrayed by [[superstring theory]], with which it closely agrees, and includes concepts such as souls, psychic energy, [[synchronicity]] (a concept originally from [[Carl Jung]], which says that things that happen at the same time are related), and ideas from quantum and theoretical physics (such as that time doesn't exist as we think it does). ==See also== *[[Edgar Cayce on Karma]] *[[Just-world phenomenon]] *[[Karma in Hinduism]] *[[Sin]] *[[Theosophy]] *[[Yuanfen]] *[[Esoteric Christianity]] ===References and Related Links=== † Cited from ''Dancing with Siva'' by [[Satguru Sivaya Subramuniyaswami]] *[http://www.veda.harekrsna.cz/encyclopedia/dharma.htm Dharma-Karma-Samsara] *[http://www.lioncity.net/buddhism/lofiversion/index.php/t10692.html Karma In Buddhism] *[http://swami-center.org/en/chpt/ecology/page_7.shtml Destiny and Its Correction] *[http://www.exoticindiaart.com/article/karma Exploring Karma - Tales of a Universal Principle] *[http://www.photonics.cusat.edu/article2.html Karma and the laws of Quantam Mechanics] *[http://www.lawofkarma.net/lpjarun/index.html Law of Karma - Dhamma Practice Book Series, by Luang Poh Jarun of Wat Amphawan, Thailand]

Societal groups as nations and their populations incur collective karma, and personalities incur individual karma. ====Three Kinds of Karma==== * There are three types of karma, *# [[sanchita karma]], the sum total of past karmas yet to be resolved; *# [[prarabdha karma]], that portion of sanchita karma that is to be experienced in this life; and *# [[kriyamana karma]], the karma that humans are currently creating and will bear fruit in the future. Notably, Karma in Hinduism, which differs from Buddhism and Jainism, involves the role of [[God]]. For a detailed look at such a role, please see [[Karma in Hinduism]]. ===Buddhism=== In Buddhism, only intentional actions are karmic "acts of [[Will (philosophy)|will]]". The 'Law of Karma' refers to "cause and effect", but Karma literally means "action" - often indicating intent or cause. Accompanying this usually is a separate tenet called [[Vipaka]], meaning result or effect. The re-action or effect can itself also influence an action, and in this way, the chain of causation continues [[ad infinitum]]. When Buddhists talk about karma, they are normally referring to karma/action that is 'tainted' with ignorance - karma that continues to ensure that the being remains in the everlasting cycle of [[samsara]]. This samsaric karma comes in two 'flavours' - 'good' karma, which leads to positive/pleasurable experiences, like high rebirth (as a [[deva]], [[asura]], or [[human]]), and bad karma which leads to suffering and low rebirth (as a [[hell]]-sufferer, as a [[preta]], or as an animal). There is also a completely different type of karma that is neither good nor bad, but liberating. This karma allows for the individual to break the uncontrolled cycle of rebirth which always implies suffering, and thereby leave [[samsara]] to permanently enter [[Nirvana]]. The Buddhist [[sutra]]s explain that in order to generate liberating karma, we must first develop incredibly powerful concentration, and proper insight into the (un)reality of samsara. This concentration is akin to the states of mind required to be reborn in the Deva realm, and in itself depends upon a very deep training in ethical self-discipline. This differentiation between good karma and liberating karma has been used by some scholars to argue that the development of [[Tantra]] depended upon Buddhist ideas and philosophies. Karma is related to the notion of [[Rebirth (Buddhist)|Buddhist rebirth]] - sometimes understood to be the same thing as [[reincarnation]] - which has its roots in the principle of Karma. ===Jainism=== Jains believe that karma is a form of [[matter]]. [[Mahavira]] described karma as "[[clay]] [[particle]]s". Jains do not believe in "good karma" or "bad karma"; they try to avoid all karma. ===Parallels with Christianity=== [[Christian]] teachings do not usually include the idea of Karma, although some parallels can be made, such as in the [[ethic of reciprocity|Golden Rule]] and as exemplified by biblical verses: :God is not mocked, what a man sows he must reap ''and'' "[[Vengeance]] is mine" says the Lord. Christianity is saturated with the concept of poetic justice not only from scripture but also in colloquialisms such as: "What goes around comes around." "Good things happen to good people." "You reap what you sow." Karma is thought by some [[Society of Jesus|Jesuit]] theologians to be consistent with the doctrine of [[Purgatory|purgatory]]. For other Christians however, the idea of the [[Abrahamic God]] makes the concept of Karma redundant. Most interpretations of [[Christianity]] do not emphasize the religious importance of thoughts and intentions ([[volition]]), that are usually understood to be a major form of Karma by the doctrines that use that concept. From the Bible we read: "For as he thinketh in his heart, so is he." (Proverbs 23:7) From the Book of Mormon we read: "But this much I can tell you, that if ye do not watch yourselves, and your thoughts, and your words, and your deeds . . . ye must perish. And now, O man, remember, and perish not." (Mosiah 4:30) ===Surat Shabda Yoga=== The [[Surat Shabd Yoga|Surat Shabda Yoga]] traditions describe four types of karma. To those listed under ''[[#Three Kinds of Karma|Three Kinds of Karma]]'' (above), it adds: Adi karma (original karma)—karma not earned but given by the Divine as the soul descends into the lower creation. == Western Interpretation == An academic and religious definition was mentioned above. Although Karma cannot be proven as easily as the law of [[gravity]], millions of people believe in it and is a part of many cultures and the psyches of millions of people. Others without religious backgrounds, especially in western cultures or with Christian upbringings, become convinced of the existence of Karma. For some, karma is a more reasonable concept than eternal damnation for the wicked. [[Spirituality]] or a belief that virtue is rewarded and sin creates suffering eventually leads to a belief in Karma. According to Karma, performance of positive action results with the reaction of a good conditioning in one's experience, whereas a negative action results in a reaction of a bad response. This may be an immediate result following the act, or a delayed result occurring either in the present life or the next. Thus, meritorious acts may create rebirth into a higher station, such as a superior human being or a godlike being, while evil acts result in rebirth as a human living in less desirable circumstances, or as a lower animal. Some observers have compared the action of karma to [[Western civilization|Western]] notions of [[sin]] and judgment by [[God]] or gods, while others understand karma as an inherent principle of the Universe without the intervention of any supernatural Being. In [[Hinduism]], God does play a role and is seen as a dispenser of karma; see [[Karma in Hinduism]] for more details. The latter understanding is accurate with regard to [[Buddhism]] and [[Jainism]]. Most teachings say that for common mortals, having an involvement with Karma is an unavoidable part of day-to-day living. However, in light of the Hindu philosophical school of [[Vedanta]], as well as [[Gautama Buddha]]'s teachings, one is advised to either avoid, control or become mindful of the effects of desires and aversions as a way to moderate or change one's karma (or, more accurately, one's karmic results). ===New Age and Theosophy=== The idea of karma was popularized in the west through the work of the [[Theosophical Society]]. [[Kardecist Spiritualism|Kardecist]] and Western [[New Age]] reinterpretations of karma frequently cast it as a sort of luck which is associated with virtue: if one does good or spiritually valuable acts, one deserves and can expect good luck; conversely, if one does harmful things, one can expect bad luck or unfortunate happenings. In this conception, karma is affiliated with the [[Neopaganism|Neopagan]] ''law of return'' or ''Threefold Law,'' the idea that the beneficial or harmful effects one has on the world will return to oneself. There's also the metaphysical idea that, because karma is a force of nature and not a sentient creature capable of making value judgments, karma isn't about good and evil deeds, since applying those labels would require those judgments, but about positive and negative energy, where negative energy can include things not seen as "being bad" like sadness and fear, and positive energy can be caused by being creative and solving problems as well as by exuding love and doing virtuous acts. This conception of karma handles the big problem with the more traditional view, because it explains why bad things happen to people who've done nothing "wrong"; it's all due to the sort of energy they've sent out into the universe with their thoughts and feelings, which exert as much power as actual actions. This view of karma, which centers around the idea that all things are made of karmic energy and thus able to affect each other, is referred to as "omniverse karma" or "omni-karma" because it requires the existence of an [[omniverse]] (a space which contains all the universes) as portrayed by [[superstring theory]], with which it closely agrees, and includes concepts such as souls, psychic energy, [[synchronicity]] (a concept originally from [[Carl Jung]], which says that things that happen at the same time are related), and ideas from quantum and theoretical physics (such as that time doesn't exist as we think it does). ==See also== *[[Edgar Cayce on Karma]] *[[Just-world phenomenon]] *[[Karma in Hinduism]] *[[Sin]] *[[Theosophy]] *[[Yuanfen]] *[[Esoteric Christianity]] ===References and Related Links=== † Cited from ''Dancing with Siva'' by [[Satguru Sivaya Subramuniyaswami]] *[http://www.veda.harekrsna.cz/encyclopedia/dharma.htm Dharma-Karma-Samsara] *[http://www.lioncity.net/buddhism/lofiversion/index.php/t10692.html Karma In Buddhism] *[http://swami-center.org/en/chpt/ecology/page_7.shtml Destiny and Its Correction] *[http://www.exoticindiaart.com/article/karma Exploring Karma - Tales of a Universal Principle] *[http://www.photonics.cusat.edu/article2.html Karma and the laws of Quantam Mechanics] *[http://www.lawofkarma.net/lpjarun/index.html Law of Karma - Dhamma Practice Book Series, by Luang Poh Jarun of Wat Amphawan, Thailand]

However, in light of the Hindu philosophical school of [[Vedanta]], as well as [[Gautama Buddha]]'s teachings, one is advised to either avoid, control or become mindful of the effects of desires and aversions as a way to moderate or change one's karma (or, more accurately, one's karmic results). ===New Age and Theosophy=== The idea of karma was popularized in the west through the work of the [[Theosophical Society]]. In this conception, karma is affiliated with the [[Neopaganism|Neopagan]] ''law of return'' or ''Threefold Law,'' the idea that the beneficial or harmful effects one has on the world will return to oneself. There's also the metaphysical idea that, because karma is a force of nature and not a sentient creature capable of making value judgments, karma isn't about good and evil deeds, since applying those labels would require those judgments, but about positive and negative energy, where negative energy can include things not seen as "being bad" like sadness and fear, and positive energy can be caused by being creative and solving problems as well as by exuding love and doing virtuous acts. This conception of karma handles the big problem with the more traditional view, because it explains why bad things happen to people who've done nothing "wrong"; it's all due to the sort of energy they've sent out into the universe with their thoughts and feelings, which exert as much power as actual actions. This view of karma, which centers around the idea that all things are made of karmic energy and thus able to affect each other, is referred to as "omniverse karma" or "omni-karma" because it requires the existence of an [[omniverse]] (a space which contains all the universes) as portrayed by [[superstring theory]], with which it closely agrees, and includes concepts such as souls, psychic energy, [[synchronicity]] (a concept originally from [[Carl Jung]], which says that things that happen at the same time are related), and ideas from quantum and theoretical physics (such as that time doesn't exist as we think it does). ==See also== *[[Edgar Cayce on Karma]] *[[Just-world phenomenon]] *[[Karma in Hinduism]] *[[Sin]] *[[Theosophy]] *[[Yuanfen]] *[[Esoteric Christianity]] ===References and Related Links=== † Cited from ''Dancing with Siva'' by [[Satguru Sivaya Subramuniyaswami]] *[http://www.veda.harekrsna.cz/encyclopedia/dharma.htm Dharma-Karma-Samsara] *[http://www.lioncity.net/buddhism/lofiversion/index.php/t10692.html Karma In Buddhism] *[http://swami-center.org/en/chpt/ecology/page_7.shtml Destiny and Its Correction] *[http://www.exoticindiaart.com/article/karma Exploring Karma - Tales of a Universal Principle] *[http://www.photonics.cusat.edu/article2.html Karma and the laws of Quantam Mechanics] *[http://www.lawofkarma.net/lpjarun/index.html Law of Karma - Dhamma Practice Book Series, by Luang Poh Jarun of Wat Amphawan, Thailand]

:''This article is about the religious concept. For other uses, see [[Karma (disambiguation)]]'' :''Basic definition'': '''Karma''' is a concept of [[eastern religions]] about the entire cycle of [[cause and effect]]. Simply explained, it is a sum of all that an individual has once done during many lives and is currently doing. The effects of those deeds actively create present and future experiences, thus making one responsible for one's own life. '''Karma''' ([[Sanskrit]]: कर्म from the root kri, "to do", meaning ''deed'') or '''Kamma''' ([[Pali]]: meaning ''action, effect, destiny''). In Hinduism and, later, Buddhism, it is the sum of a person's actions, regarded as determining that person's future states of existence. The law of '''Karma''' originated in the [[Vedic religion|Vedic]] system of religion, otherwise known as [[Hinduism]] or ''Sanatan Dharma'' (perennial faith). As a term, it can at the latest be traced back to the early [[Upanishads]], around [[1500s BC|1500 BC]]. == Karma in the [[Dharma]]-based religions == ===Hinduism=== :''See main article, [[Karma in Hinduism]]'' The concept of Karma, based on the [[Vedas]] and [[Upanishads]] was a concept that was adopted by other religions like [[Buddhism]] and [[Jainism]]. One of the first and most dramatic illustrations of Karma can be found in the great Hindu [[epic]], the [[Mahabharata]]. The original Hindu concept of karma was later enhanced by several other movements within the religion, most notably [[Vedanta]], and [[Tantra]]. Karma literally means "deed" or "act" and more broadly names the universal principle of [[cause]] and [[effect]], action and reaction which governs all life. Karma is not fate, for man acts with free will creating his own destiny. According to the Vedas, if we sow [[Goodness and value theory|goodness]], we will reap goodness; if we sow [[evil]], we will reap evil. Karma refers to the totality of our actions and their concomitant reactions in this and previous lives, all of which determines our future. The conquest of karma lies in intelligent action and dispassionate reaction. Not all karmas rebound immediately. Some accumulate and return unexpectedly in this or other births. As †Satguru Sivaya Subramuniyaswami explains it, unkindness yields spoiled fruits, called [[papa]] and good deeds bring forth sweet fruits, called [[punya]]. He further notes that as one acts, so does he become. One becomes virtuous by virtuous action, bad by bad action. It is considered an entirely impersonal and spiritually originated law that cannot be abrogated by any person. The thought of karma as punishment or being retributive is incorrect, as it is simply an extended expression of natural acts. The effects experienced are also able to be mitigated by actions and are not necessarily fateful. Societal groups as nations and their populations incur collective karma, and personalities incur individual karma. ====Three Kinds of Karma==== * There are three types of karma, *# [[sanchita karma]], the sum total of past karmas yet to be resolved; *# [[prarabdha karma]], that portion of sanchita karma that is to be experienced in this life; and *# [[kriyamana karma]], the karma that humans are currently creating and will bear fruit in the future. Notably, Karma in Hinduism, which differs from Buddhism and Jainism, involves the role of [[God]]. For a detailed look at such a role, please see [[Karma in Hinduism]]. ===Buddhism=== In Buddhism, only intentional actions are karmic "acts of [[Will (philosophy)|will]]". The 'Law of Karma' refers to "cause and effect", but Karma literally means "action" - often indicating intent or cause. Accompanying this usually is a separate tenet called [[Vipaka]], meaning result or effect. The re-action or effect can itself also influence an action, and in this way, the chain of causation continues [[ad infinitum]]. When Buddhists talk about karma, they are normally referring to karma/action that is 'tainted' with ignorance - karma that continues to ensure that the being remains in the everlasting cycle of [[samsara]]. This samsaric karma comes in two 'flavours' - 'good' karma, which leads to positive/pleasurable experiences, like high rebirth (as a [[deva]], [[asura]], or [[human]]), and bad karma which leads to suffering and low rebirth (as a [[hell]]-sufferer, as a [[preta]], or as an animal). There is also a completely different type of karma that is neither good nor bad, but liberating. This karma allows for the individual to break the uncontrolled cycle of rebirth which always implies suffering, and thereby leave [[samsara]] to permanently enter [[Nirvana]]. The Buddhist [[sutra]]s explain that in order to generate liberating karma, we must first develop incredibly powerful concentration, and proper insight into the (un)reality of samsara. This concentration is akin to the states of mind required to be reborn in the Deva realm, and in itself depends upon a very deep training in ethical self-discipline. This differentiation between good karma and liberating karma has been used by some scholars to argue that the development of [[Tantra]] depended upon Buddhist ideas and philosophies. Karma is related to the notion of [[Rebirth (Buddhist)|Buddhist rebirth]] - sometimes understood to be the same thing as [[reincarnation]] - which has its roots in the principle of Karma. ===Jainism=== Jains believe that karma is a form of [[matter]]. [[Mahavira]] described karma as "[[clay]] [[particle]]s". Jains do not believe in "good karma" or "bad karma"; they try to avoid all karma. ===Parallels with Christianity=== [[Christian]] teachings do not usually include the idea of Karma, although some parallels can be made, such as in the [[ethic of reciprocity|Golden Rule]] and as exemplified by biblical verses: :God is not mocked, what a man sows he must reap ''and'' "[[Vengeance]] is mine" says the Lord. Christianity is saturated with the concept of poetic justice not only from scripture but also in colloquialisms such as: "What goes around comes around." "Good things happen to good people." "You reap what you sow." Karma is thought by some [[Society of Jesus|Jesuit]] theologians to be consistent with the doctrine of [[Purgatory|purgatory]]. For other Christians however, the idea of the [[Abrahamic God]] makes the concept of Karma redundant. Most interpretations of [[Christianity]] do not emphasize the religious importance of thoughts and intentions ([[volition]]), that are usually understood to be a major form of Karma by the doctrines that use that concept. From the Bible we read: "For as he thinketh in his heart, so is he." (Proverbs 23:7) From the Book of Mormon we read: "But this much I can tell you, that if ye do not watch yourselves, and your thoughts, and your words, and your deeds . . . ye must perish. And now, O man, remember, and perish not." (Mosiah 4:30) ===Surat Shabda Yoga=== The [[Surat Shabd Yoga|Surat Shabda Yoga]] traditions describe four types of karma. To those listed under ''[[#Three Kinds of Karma|Three Kinds of Karma]]'' (above), it adds: Adi karma (original karma)—karma not earned but given by the Divine as the soul descends into the lower creation. == Western Interpretation == An academic and religious definition was mentioned above. Although Karma cannot be proven as easily as the law of [[gravity]], millions of people believe in it and is a part of many cultures and the psyches of millions of people. Others without religious backgrounds, especially in western cultures or with Christian upbringings, become convinced of the existence of Karma. For some, karma is a more reasonable concept than eternal damnation for the wicked. [[Spirituality]] or a belief that virtue is rewarded and sin creates suffering eventually leads to a belief in Karma. According to Karma, performance of positive action results with the reaction of a good conditioning in one's experience, whereas a negative action results in a reaction of a bad response. This may be an immediate result following the act, or a delayed result occurring either in the present life or the next. Thus, meritorious acts may create rebirth into a higher station, such as a superior human being or a godlike being, while evil acts result in rebirth as a human living in less desirable circumstances, or as a lower animal. Some observers have compared the action of karma to [[Western civilization|Western]] notions of [[sin]] and judgment by [[God]] or gods, while others understand karma as an inherent principle of the Universe without the intervention of any supernatural Being. In [[Hinduism]], God does play a role and is seen as a dispenser of karma; see [[Karma in Hinduism]] for more details. The latter understanding is accurate with regard to [[Buddhism]] and [[Jainism]]. Most teachings say that for common mortals, having an involvement with Karma is an unavoidable part of day-to-day living. However, in light of the Hindu philosophical school of [[Vedanta]], as well as [[Gautama Buddha]]'s teachings, one is advised to either avoid, control or become mindful of the effects of desires and aversions as a way to moderate or change one's karma (or, more accurately, one's karmic results). ===New Age and Theosophy=== The idea of karma was popularized in the west through the work of the [[Theosophical Society]]. [[Kardecist Spiritualism|Kardecist]] and Western [[New Age]] reinterpretations of karma frequently cast it as a sort of luck which is associated with virtue: if one does good or spiritually valuable acts, one deserves and can expect good luck; conversely, if one does harmful things, one can expect bad luck or unfortunate happenings. In this conception, karma is affiliated with the [[Neopaganism|Neopagan]] ''law of return'' or ''Threefold Law,'' the idea that the beneficial or harmful effects one has on the world will return to oneself. There's also the metaphysical idea that, because karma is a force of nature and not a sentient creature capable of making value judgments, karma isn't about good and evil deeds, since applying those labels would require those judgments, but about positive and negative energy, where negative energy can include things not seen as "being bad" like sadness and fear, and positive energy can be caused by being creative and solving problems as well as by exuding love and doing virtuous acts. This conception of karma handles the big problem with the more traditional view, because it explains why bad things happen to people who've done nothing "wrong"; it's all due to the sort of energy they've sent out into the universe with their thoughts and feelings, which exert as much power as actual actions. This view of karma, which centers around the idea that all things are made of karmic energy and thus able to affect each other, is referred to as "omniverse karma" or "omni-karma" because it requires the existence of an [[omniverse]] (a space which contains all the universes) as portrayed by [[superstring theory]], with which it closely agrees, and includes concepts such as souls, psychic energy, [[synchronicity]] (a concept originally from [[Carl Jung]], which says that things that happen at the same time are related), and ideas from quantum and theoretical physics (such as that time doesn't exist as we think it does). ==See also== *[[Edgar Cayce on Karma]] *[[Just-world phenomenon]] *[[Karma in Hinduism]] *[[Sin]] *[[Theosophy]] *[[Yuanfen]] *[[Esoteric Christianity]] ===References and Related Links=== † Cited from ''Dancing with Siva'' by [[Satguru Sivaya Subramuniyaswami]] *[http://www.veda.harekrsna.cz/encyclopedia/dharma.htm Dharma-Karma-Samsara] *[http://www.lioncity.net/buddhism/lofiversion/index.php/t10692.html Karma In Buddhism] *[http://swami-center.org/en/chpt/ecology/page_7.shtml Destiny and Its Correction] *[http://www.exoticindiaart.com/article/karma Exploring Karma - Tales of a Universal Principle] *[http://www.photonics.cusat.edu/article2.html Karma and the laws of Quantam Mechanics] *[http://www.lawofkarma.net/v1_regular/lpjarun/index.html Law of Karma - Dhamma Practice Book Series, by Luang Poh Jarun of Wat Amphawan, Thailand]

According to the Vedas, if we sow [[Goodness and value theory|goodness]], we will reap goodness; if we sow [[evil]], we will reap evil. Karma refers to the totality of our actions and their concomitant reactions in this and previous lives, all of which determines our future. The conquest of karma lies in intelligent action and dispassionate reaction. Not all karmas rebound immediately. Some accumulate and return unexpectedly in this or other births. As †Satguru Sivaya Subramuniyaswami explains it, unkindness yields spoiled fruits, called [[papa]] and good deeds bring forth sweet fruits, called [[punya]]. He further notes that as one acts, so does he become. One becomes virtuous by virtuous action, bad by bad action. It is considered an entirely impersonal and spiritually originated law that cannot be abrogated by any person. The thought of karma as punishment or being retributive is incorrect, as it is simply an extended expression of natural acts. The effects experienced are also able to be mitigated by actions and are not necessarily fateful. Societal groups as nations and their populations incur collective karma, and personalities incur individual karma. ====Three Kinds of Karma==== * There are three types of karma, *# [[sanchita karma]], the sum total of past karmas yet to be resolved; *# [[prarabdha karma]], that portion of sanchita karma that is to be experienced in this life; and *# [[kriyamana karma]], the karma that humans are currently creating and will bear fruit in the future. Notably, Karma in Hinduism, which differs from Buddhism and Jainism, involves the role of [[God]]. For a detailed look at such a role, please see [[Karma in Hinduism]]. ===Buddhism=== In Buddhism, only intentional actions are karmic "acts of [[Will (philosophy)|will]]". The 'Law of Karma' refers to "cause and effect", but Karma literally means "action" - often indicating intent or cause. Accompanying this usually is a separate tenet called [[Vipaka]], meaning result or effect. The re-action or effect can itself also influence an action, and in this way, the chain of causation continues [[ad infinitum]]. When Buddhists talk about karma, they are normally referring to karma/action that is 'tainted' with ignorance - karma that continues to ensure that the being remains in the everlasting cycle of [[samsara]]. This samsaric karma comes in two 'flavours' - 'good' karma, which leads to positive/pleasurable experiences, like high rebirth (as a [[deva]], [[asura]], or [[human]]), and bad karma which leads to suffering and low rebirth (as a [[hell]]-sufferer, as a [[preta]], or as an animal). There is also a completely different type of karma that is neither good nor bad, but liberating. This karma allows for the individual to break the uncontrolled cycle of rebirth which always implies suffering, and thereby leave [[samsara]] to permanently enter [[Nirvana]]. The Buddhist [[sutra]]s explain that in order to generate liberating karma, we must first develop incredibly powerful concentration, and proper insight into the (un)reality of samsara. This concentration is akin to the states of mind required to be reborn in the Deva realm, and in itself depends upon a very deep training in ethical self-discipline. This differentiation between good karma and liberating karma has been used by some scholars to argue that the development of [[Tantra]] depended upon Buddhist ideas and philosophies. Karma is related to the notion of [[Rebirth (Buddhist)|Buddhist rebirth]] - sometimes understood to be the same thing as [[reincarnation]] - which has its roots in the principle of Karma. ===Jainism=== Jains believe that karma is a form of [[matter]]. [[Mahavira]] described karma as "[[clay]] [[particle]]s". Jains do not believe in "good karma" or "bad karma"; they try to avoid all karma. ===Parallels with Christianity=== [[Christian]] teachings do not usually include the idea of Karma, although some parallels can be made, such as in the [[ethic of reciprocity|Golden Rule]] and as exemplified by biblical verses: :God is not mocked, what a man sows he must reap ''and'' "[[Vengeance]] is mine" says the Lord. Christianity is saturated with the concept of poetic justice not only from scripture but also in colloquialisms such as: "What goes around comes around." "Good things happen to good people." "You reap what you sow." Karma is thought by some [[Society of Jesus|Jesuit]] theologians to be consistent with the doctrine of [[Purgatory|purgatory]]. For other Christians however, the idea of the [[Abrahamic God]] makes the concept of Karma redundant. Most interpretations of [[Christianity]] do not emphasize the religious importance of thoughts and intentions ([[volition]]), that are usually understood to be a major form of Karma by the doctrines that use that concept. From the Bible we read: "For as he thinketh in his heart, so is he." (Proverbs 23:7) From the Book of Mormon we read: "But this much I can tell you, that if ye do not watch yourselves, and your thoughts, and your words, and your deeds . . . ye must perish. And now, O man, remember, and perish not." (Mosiah 4:30) ===Surat Shabda Yoga=== The [[Surat Shabd Yoga|Surat Shabda Yoga]] traditions describe four types of karma. To those listed under ''[[#Three Kinds of Karma|Three Kinds of Karma]]'' (above), it adds: Adi karma (original karma)—karma not earned but given by the Divine as the soul descends into the lower creation. == Western Interpretation == An academic and religious definition was mentioned above. Although Karma cannot be proven as easily as the law of [[gravity]], millions of people believe in it and is a part of many cultures and the psyches of millions of people. Others without religious backgrounds, especially in western cultures or with Christian upbringings, become convinced of the existence of Karma. For some, karma is a more reasonable concept than eternal damnation for the wicked. [[Spirituality]] or a belief that virtue is rewarded and sin creates suffering eventually leads to a belief in Karma. According to Karma, performance of positive action results with the reaction of a good conditioning in one's experience, whereas a negative action results in a reaction of a bad response. This may be an immediate result following the act, or a delayed result occurring either in the present life or the next. Thus, meritorious acts may create rebirth into a higher station, such as a superior human being or a godlike being, while evil acts result in rebirth as a human living in less desirable circumstances, or as a lower animal. Some observers have compared the action of karma to [[Western civilization|Western]] notions of [[sin]] and judgment by [[God]] or gods, while others understand karma as an inherent principle of the Universe without the intervention of any supernatural Being. In [[Hinduism]], God does play a role and is seen as a dispenser of karma; see [[Karma in Hinduism]] for more details. The latter understanding is accurate with regard to [[Buddhism]] and [[Jainism]]. Most teachings say that for common mortals, having an involvement with Karma is an unavoidable part of day-to-day living. However, in light of the Hindu philosophical school of [[Vedanta]], as well as [[Gautama Buddha]]'s teachings, one is advised to either avoid, control or become mindful of the effects of desires and aversions as a way to moderate or change one's karma (or, more accurately, one's karmic results). ===New Age and Theosophy=== The idea of karma was popularized in the west through the work of the [[Theosophical Society]]. [[Kardecist Spiritualism|Kardecist]] and Western [[New Age]] reinterpretations of karma frequently cast it as a sort of luck which is associated with virtue: if one does good or spiritually valuable acts, one deserves and can expect good luck; conversely, if one does harmful things, one can expect bad luck or unfortunate happenings. In this conception, karma is affiliated with the [[Neopaganism|Neopagan]] ''law of return'' or ''Threefold Law,'' the idea that the beneficial or harmful effects one has on the world will return to oneself. There's also the metaphysical idea that, because karma is a force of nature and not a sentient creature capable of making value judgments, karma isn't about good and evil deeds, since applying those labels would require those judgments, but about positive and negative energy, where negative energy can include things not seen as "being bad" like sadness and fear, and positive energy can be caused by being creative and solving problems as well as by exuding love and doing virtuous acts. This conception of karma handles the big problem with the more traditional view, because it explains why bad things happen to people who've done nothing "wrong"; it's all due to the sort of energy they've sent out into the universe with their thoughts and feelings, which exert as much power as actual actions. This view of karma, which centers around the idea that all things are made of karmic energy and thus able to affect each other, is referred to as "omniverse karma" or "omni-karma" because it requires the existence of an [[omniverse]] (a space which contains all the universes) as portrayed by [[superstring theory]], with which it closely agrees, and includes concepts such as souls, psychic energy, [[synchronicity]] (a concept originally from [[Carl Jung]], which says that things that happen at the same time are related), and ideas from quantum and theoretical physics (such as that time doesn't exist as we think it does). ==See also== *[[Edgar Cayce on Karma]] *[[Just-world phenomenon]] *[[Karma in Hinduism]] *[[Sin]] *[[Theosophy]] *[[Yuanfen]] *[[Esoteric Christianity]] ===References and Related Links=== † Cited from ''Dancing with Siva'' by [[Satguru Sivaya Subramuniyaswami]] *[http://www.veda.harekrsna.cz/encyclopedia/dharma.htm Dharma-Karma-Samsara] *[http://www.lioncity.net/buddhism/lofiversion/index.php/t10692.html Karma In Buddhism] *[http://swami-center.org/en/chpt/ecology/page_7.shtml Destiny and Its Correction] *[http://www.exoticindiaart.com/article/karma Exploring Karma - Tales of a Universal Principle] *[http://www.photonics.cusat.edu/article2.html Karma and the laws of Quantam Mechanics] *[http://www.lawofkarma.net/v1_regular/lpjarun/index.html Law of Karma - Dhamma Practice Book Series, by Luang Poh Jarun of Wat Amphawan, Thailand]

:''Basic definition'': '''Karma''' is a concept of [[eastern religions]] about the entire cycle of [[cause and effect]]. Simply explained, it is a sum of all that an individual has once done during many lives and is currently doing. The effects of those deeds actively create present and future experiences, thus making one responsible for one's own life.
'''Karma''' ([[Sanskrit]]: कर्म from the root kri, "to do", meaning ''deed'') or '''Kamma''' ([[Pali]]: meaning ''action, effect, destiny''). In Hinduism and, later, Buddhism, it is the sum of a person's actions, regarded as determining that person's future states of existence. The law of '''Karma''' originated in the [[Vedic religion|Vedic]] system of religion, otherwise known as [[Hinduism]] or ''Sanatan Dharma'' (perennial faith). As a term, it can at the latest be traced back to the early [[Upanishads]], around [[1500s BC|1500 BC]].

Law of Karma By Luang Poh Jarun Thitadhammo
Introduction
In the present day people are starting to have doubts about the law of karma. Some people refuse to believe it altogether, up to the point where a verse was circulated around saying, "Where exists such a person who reaps good results from good deeds? But there are plenty of those who reap good results from bad deeds." Regarding the law of karma, there are five kinds of dangers facing world beings:
Kilesanataraya: the danger that arises from defilements.
Kammanataraya: the danger that arises from bad deeds being performed in the present.
Vipakanataraya: the danger that arises from the fruits of karma done in the past.
Ditthanataraya: the danger that arises from wrong view.
Ariyupavanataraya: the danger that arises from offending a Noble One.
The Buddhist religion teaches that whether an individual will reap good or bad results, whether they will meet with happiness or suffering, depends on karma, which is entirely one's own doing. If we don't live our lives according to the teachings of the Buddha, no matter how much we beg or do the chantings, we won't be able to meet with goodness and happiness. If human beings can meet with happiness by just being devoted and begging, we probably won't have to do anything.
Faith in the Law of Karma
According to the teachings of the Buddha, Buddhists should have the following four kinds of faith: Tathagatabodhi-saddha: faith in the enlightenment of the Buddha, which means to believe that the Buddha had truly attained enlightenment and is possessed of wisdom, purity and great compassion. Kamma-saddha: faith in the law of karma, which means to believe that there are good and bad deeds. Vipaka-saddha: faith in the fruits of karma, which means to believe that there are results of good and bad deeds. Kammassakata-saddha: faith that beings are owner of their karma, which means to believe that the fruits which we reap are the fruits of our own actions, which could be karma that was performed in this lifetime or in a previous lifetime.
We can see that among the four kinds of faith, three of them are related to karma. Therefore, the law of karma is an important teaching in the Buddhist religion. Every Buddhist then should believe in the law of karma. They should try to study and understand the law of karma. Buddhists who don't believe in the law of karma are not true Buddhists, but are only Buddhists by name. The Buddhist religion is only useful to them when they fill out forms so no one will accuse them of not having a religion.
People who believe in karma have an advantage over those who don't. People who believe in karma are able to endure through suffering, hardships, disappointments, coercion and misfortunes that occur to them, because they consider it the result of their past karma. They won't complain that this world is unfair, that they didn't receive justice, that they do good things but don't reap the corresponding rewards. People who believe in karma will hold tightly to the cultivation of goodness from then onwards. They will be able to forgive others and will be possessed of shame and fear of wrongdoing (hiri-ottappa).
Most people who perform unwholesome deeds by body, speech and mind in general are people who don't believe in karma, in merit and demerit, or in rebirth. These types of people therefore search for wealth and comfort for themselves, without considering whether the wealth or the enjoyment they have obtained were obtained rightfully or wrongfully, and without considering whether or not they have caused others trouble.
All beings are owner of their karma. The karma is especially ours, and we will be the ones to reap the result of that karma. We can't transfer them to other people. For example, if we perform an unwholesome karma, we will be the ones to reap the results of that unwholesome karma. We can't erase it nor can we transfer it to someone else, even if that person is willing to accept the transfer. The same goes for wholesome karma. The person who performs a wholesome deed will be the owner of that wholesome karma. We can't hire or ask someone to perform them for use. For example, we can't hire a person to perform wholesome karma and ask that person to transfer that wholesome karma to us. If we want to be its owner, we have to perform that wholesome karma ourselves. It is like having food, only people who eat will be full.
Each human existence is different. People may be good or bad, rich or poor, prosperous or unsuccessful, happy or suffering, and all completely depending on their own karma. And whichever karma we perform, good or bad, will inevitably bear fruit, and it will follow its doer like their shadow, like the wheel of the ox-cart that turns after the footprint of the ox. Therefore, human beings have karma as their refuge. If we perform wholesome karma, we will reap happiness and prosperity. Therefore, wholesome karma is like a good friend (kalyana-mitta) who is always helping and supporting us so that we meet with happiness and prosperity. But if we perform unwholesome karma, then that unwholesome karma will destroy us, causing us to meet with suffering and failure.
Types of Karma
Most people understand that karma is action. This understanding is not wrong, but it is still not thorough and completely correct, because there are certain types of action that are not considered to be karma. True karma must consist of two characteristics: The doer must have the intention. That action must result in merit or demerit. This is in accordance with the Nibbedhikpariyaya Sutta, Chakkanipata, of the Anguttara Nikaya, where the Lord Buddha said: "Cetanaham bhikkhave kammam vadami." "Volition, bhikkhus, is karma, I declare."
Volition is intention or acknowledgement which can be divided into three types:
Puraba-cetana: the volition before the action.
Muñcana-cetana: the volition in the midst of that action.
Aparapara-cetana: the volition after that action.
An action that has volition arising at one time or another is considered to be karma. On the other hand, an action that is void of volition, which means the mind didn't order the action, is not categorized as karma. For example, when a person has a high fever and becomes delirious, it is not karma if that person speaks harshly or if their hand or foot accidentally hits another person. The Vinaya makes an exception to monks who are mentally deranged, that if they were to offend against any of the training rules, they don't have to make a confession. All this is by the principle that if the doer has no volition in performing an action then that action is not karma.
The second principle which says that the action must result in merit or demerit, is to distinguish between actions performed by an Arahant and those performed by a worlding (puthujjana). As an Arahant is freed from the taints and defilements and do not cling to a self, their action is called indeterminate (abyakata). It is neither wholesome or unwholesome karma, and therefore there is no merit or demerit. So the actions performed by an Arahant is not called karma but instead it is called karmically inoperative (kiriya). On the other hand, worldlings still cling to a self, and so whatever they do they still hold onto the view that they are the one performing that action. The actions performed by a worldling, therefore, is karma that will inevitably bear fruit. Wholesome karma will result in merit, while unwholesome karma will result in demerit.
Some people believe that karma is something bad[1], along the lines of retribution and demerit. This is what is referred to when we call it, for example, "karma that results in retribution" or "bad karma," as opposed to the good side which we call "merit." All this is because we have been using the word "karma" with a bad meaning. For example, when we see a person meet with misfortune and is being punished, we say that it is their karma resulting in retribution, or that they have to reap the fruit of the bad karma that they have created. But the truth of the matter is that the word "karma" is a neutral word. It refers to our action as described above, and can be good as well as bad. If it is good karma, we call it wholesome karma (kusala-kamma). If it is bad karma, we call it unwholesome karma (akusala-kamma).
Karma can be classified in many ways. If it is classified by way of action, there are three types of karma:
Kaya-kamma: karma performed by the body.
Vacika-kamma: karma performed verbally.
Mano-kamma: karma performed mentally.
The ten courses of action categorize these three types of karma into unwholesome and wholesome karma. Karma performed by the body can be categorized in three ways for both unwholesome and wholesome karma: Unwholesome karma: killing, stealing and sexual misconduct. Wholesome karma: abstaining from killing, abstaining from stealing and abstaining from sexual misconduct. Karma performed verbally can be categorized in four ways for both unwholesome and wholesome karma: Unwholesome karma: false speech, malicious speech, harsh speech and idle chatter. Wholesome karma: abstaining from false speech, abstaining from malicious speech, abstaining from harsh speech and abstaining from idle chatter. Karma performed mentally can be categorized in three ways for both unwholesome and wholesome karma: Unwholesome karma: wanting what belongs to others, wishing harm to others and holding wrong views. Wholesome karma: not wanting what belongs to others, wishing others well and holding right views. As you can see, even thoughts are already considered karma, like, for example, if you think of stealing or of hurting someone else. Even though it hasn't turned into bodily action, it is still considered to be unwholesome karma, which must bear fruit. This is in contrast to punishment by the laws of the country, which can only take place when the doer has prepared or already performed the wrongful deed. Thoughts that plan to perform a wrongful deed are not a crime. The laws of the country do not punish people who only think of performing wrongful deeds because it is hard to prove people's thoughts and because they see no harm has been done. But according to the principles of karma, unwholesome thoughts are a crime, because even though no harm has been done to others, harm has already been done to the person who thought those thoughts. Therefore, the results of karma will follow. Reaping the fruits of karma has a wider boundary than punishment by the laws of the country.
Twelve Types of Karma
In the Visuddhimagga by Bhadantacariya Buddhaghosa, karma can be divided into twelve types. Karma Ripening According to Time Dittha-dhamma-vedaniya-kamma: karma ripening during this lifetime.
Upapajja-vedaniya-kamma: karma ripening in the next birth. Aparapariya-vedaniya-kamma: karma ripening in later births. Ahosi-kamma: ineffectual karma; karma that has already ripened or that is unable to produce any results in the future. Karma Ripening According to Function
Janaka-kamma: karma that was created and can be good or bad.
Upatthambhaka-kamma: supportive karma. If the original karma (janaka-kamma) was good then this supportive karma makes things even better. If the original karma was bad then this supportive karma makes things even worse.
Upapilaka-kamma: oppressive or counteractive karma; disturbs the original karma. If the original karma was good, then this counteractive karma disturbs it and makes things bad. If the original karma was bad, then this counteractive karma disturbs it and makes things good.
Upaghataka-kamma: karma that severs; it flips the situation. For example, the original karma that was created is extremely good, then this karma turns the person into a beggar or brings death. Or if the original karma that was created is extremely bad, then this karma turns the person into a king or a millionaire. Karma Ripening According to its Weight
Garuka-kamma: weighty karma. Wholesome weighty karma consists of the jhanas. Unwholesome weighty karma is performing anantarika-kamma, for example, killing parents. This karma will bear fruit and cannot be stopped by any other karma.
Bahula-kamma: karma performed habitually
Asanna-kamma: karma that was performed near death or the karma that the mind is settled on near the time of death. Asanna-kamma can result in a good or a bad rebirth. It is like an old ox standing at the entrance of the pen. Even though it has little strength but once the pen is opened, it can exit first.
Katatta-kamma: karma that is done casually, with an intention that is incomplete. It might have been done heedlessly or ignorantly. The karmic results may be good or bad, and the karma will bear fruit when there aren't any other karma ripening.
Why People Believe Doing Good Doesn't Bring Good Results
There are people who perform bad karma but it turns out that they are rich, powerful and with people who respect and praise them. As for those who work with sincerity, honesty and diligence, they are poor and living with hardships. Or some people who don't really do any work, but kiss up to and flatter their boss, get promoted and a salary raise. As for those who are earnest in their work but don't kiss up to their boss, they don't receive such good results. And so people think the law of karma doesn't exist for real, that the teaching,
"Kalyanakari kalyanam papakari ca papakam," "Do good and reap good results; do bad and reap bad results,"
is probably untrue. The reason people see that doing good you don't reap good results or that doing bad you don't reap bad results, is due a lack of understanding of the following two points: They don't understand how karma bears fruit. They don't understand the meaning of reaping good results and reaping bad results. [
How Karma Bears Fruit
There are two levels in how karma bears fruit, the ordinary level and the morality level. The karma that bears its fruit on the ordinary level, does so without consideration for the Dhamma. For example, if Mr. A cheats the government out of money or stole some wealth, Mr. A then obtains that money. And if Mr. A uses it to buy a house, Mr. A then will get to live in that house. This is how karma bears fruit on the ordinary level. But the karma doesn't stop there at bearing its fruits. That karma will bear fruit on a morality level as well, which is if we've done good, we must reap good results for sure and if we've done bad, we must reap bad results, which can't be avoided.
Some karma might bear fruit in this lifetime—this is called ditthi-dhamma-vedaniya-kamma. Some karma might bear fruit in the next life—this is called uppajja-vedaniya-kamma. Other karma might bear fruit in the lives after next—this is called aparapara-vedaniya-kamma.
In planting a vegetable or a tree, it is not as if if we were to place the seed into the earth, the vegetable or tree will sprout immediately. Some vegetables grow fast, while others grow more slowly, taking years. For example, in planting rice seeds, it would take four or five months until you see results, but in planting a coconut tree or a durian tree, it can take up to five years.
Thus, the reason people who perform bad deeds are still reaping good results is because their bad karma has not ripened. The good karma that was performed in the past is upatthambhaka-kamma that is still supporting them. The bad karma will become upaghata-kamma that will cause their situation to change from white to black, like, for example, a rich person might become poor, and a big and powerful person might become a victim of an accusation and end up behind bars or might have to run and hide from the law without a place to stay.
People who don't believe in karma often see the results of karma on an ordinary level. Their eyesight is poor, so they can't see the results of karma on a morality level. These people often don't believe in rebirth, but instead believe that this life is the only life and that's it. So when they perform some bad karma and that bad karma isn't bearing fruit, then they think that they are intelligent, and look down on those who believe in karma, saying they're stupid and foolish. These people are like those eating sweets mixed with poison; as long as the poison hasn't given its results, they think the sweets are delicious, in accordance with the Buddhist saying,
"Madhuva maññati balo yava papam na muccati." "The fool sees that evil is like honey, as long as that evil hasn't beared fruit."
The results of karma can be divided into (1) the fruits of karma in the mind and (2) the material fruits of karma.
The fruits of karma in the mind especially concern the doer of that karma, and nothing to do with other people. Once the karma is done, the doer immediately receives its fruits. This means when they perform good karma, they will receive happiness and joy; and when they perform bad karma, the mind will become depressed and will suffer. On the other hand, the material fruits of karma concern other people, and it is very difficult to get it right. People who perform good karma in hoping for material gains must fulfill four conditions:
Gati-samapati: doing it at the right place.
Upadhi-samapati: doing it for the right recipient.
Kala-samapati: doing it at the right time.
Payoga-samapati: doing it continuously.
The reason people who perform good karma hoping for material gains such as wealth, fame and praise but don't attain them as desired, could be because they didn't perform the good karma following these four conditions. This means they might have done something good with an individual that doesn't have goodness. For example, we work with sincerity and honesty but our boss is corrupt. The good we do then won't be praised by our boss. Doing good with these types of people is no different from placing a seed on a rock or on dry land. Thus, in doing good we should hope for returns in the mind more than material gains. Some people might have really done something good but it might not have reached goodness, that is, they might have done a small good deed and then hope for good results. When they don't receive good results in return, they lose heart and say that doing good doesn't seem to result in good. These people are like those who plant some seeds, water them a little, loosen the soil a little and then hope to see results.
There are differences in the meaning of receiving good and bad in the worldly way and in the way of the Dhamma. In the worldly way, the reaping of good and bad results are material concerns. When people say that that person has received good results, they often mean that that person has gained wealth and fame, such as property and power, or job promotions. When they don't receive such returns, then they understand that they didn't receive any good results. In the way of the Dhamma, the reaping of good and bad results are mind matters. Reaping good results means making the mind better, increasing the goodness within us and making the mind clearer, brighter and more peaceful. In contrast, reaping bad results means making the mind more base, worse and more gloomy. Reaping good results then refers to goodness, and reaping bad results then refers to badness. So if we were to say instead, do good and reap goodness, do bad and reap badness, then we will better understand about the reaping of good and bad results.
A person performing some karma will immediately receive results in the mind. When they perform good karma, such as making merits, giving food to monks and helping others, the mind will become better, and there will be joy and happiness from the good karma that they have done, since the karma performed is truly wholesome karma (kusala-kamma), which means it was performed with a wholesome and pure mind, and not with greed nor with an unwholesome intention, nor with a desire for something in return.
Notes
1. This is how the word "karma" is used in everyday Thai language.
